name: Lepontic
confidence_why: Stifter 2016, the leading authority on Lepontic, states outright that the stress systems of the Ancient Celtic languages are unknown and that the initial stress assumed in accentual scansions of the Vergiate and Ornavasso inscriptions is only a hypothesis, and none of the other works read (Stifter 2010, 2019, 2020, Eska 1998, the Lexicon Leponticum phonology page) says anything about stress at all.
catalog_citation: Stifter, David. 2016. Metrical systems of Celtic traditions. NOWELE - North-Western European Language Evolution 69(1): 38-94. doi:10.1075/nowele.69.1.02sti (Benjamins offprint; author-archived open access on MURAL Maynooth)
catalog_locator: p. 59, first paragraph (file page 23 of 58); Lepontic applications p. 51 (Vergiate VA·6) and p. 52 (Ornavasso VB·3.1)
catalog_quote: All approaches pose their own problems. To start with the accentual metrical approach, its fundamental weakness lies in the fact that the stress systems of Ancient Celtic languages are unknown. Only more or less sophisticated hypotheses have been proposed about their nature. In many instances where accentual metrics are involved, the implicit assumption is that the texts have to be scanned with initial dynamic stress. One argument in favour of it is the fact that alliteration, which is particularly suited for stress-initial languages, is of relatively frequent occurrence in Ancient Celtic texts. Initial stress automatically entails that the language tends towards a trochaic or dactylic rhythm in its poetry. [p. 59] ... If the poem is analysed as accentual (assuming initial stress), it can be read as having a trochaic structure (with several substitutions of dactyls for trochaei). [p. 51, on Vergiate VA·6, reporting Eska & Mercado 2005] ... The same rhythm remains if an accentual scansion with stress on the first syllable is used or superimposed on the quantitative verse [p. 52, on Ornavasso VB·3.1]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is recoverable: the source states outright that the stress system of Lepontic (and the other Ancient Celtic languages) is unknown. The working hypothesis used in metrical scholarship is initial dynamic stress, supported only indirectly by the frequency of alliteration; Stifter applies it to the Lepontic Vergiate and Ornavasso texts ('assuming initial stress', p. 51; 'an accentual scansion with stress on the first syllable', p. 52) but flags it as an assumption.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source's caveat is global (p. 59). For Ornavasso VB·3.1 (p. 52) an initial-stress scansion is shown as compatible with, not evidence for, a quantitative trochaic tetrameter.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about 'Ancient Celtic languages' collectively (Lepontic, Cisalpine Gaulish, Gaulish, Celtiberian), made in a paper on metrics, not a phonological description; evidence base is a corpus of short epigraphic texts, no citation forms. Stifter 2020 (Palaeohispanica 20, §1.4.1 Phonology) and Lexicon Leponticum's Phonology page, the only modern phonological sketches found, are silent on accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Stifter's statement (p. 59) is about the Ancient Celtic languages collectively; the Lepontic-specific applications (pp. 50-52) concern the inscriptions of Vergiate VA·6, Prestino CO·48 (both early Lepontic, pre-400 BCE in the LexLep definition) and Ornavasso VB·3.1 (late phase, 2nd/1st c. BCE, which some classify as Cisalpine Gaulish). Lexicon Leponticum restricts 'Lepontic' to pre-400 BCE texts and treats Cisalpine Gaulish as a separate language (its glottocode not checked here). The catalog entry, if made, should read 'stress system unknown (extinct, epigraphic); initial dynamic stress is the working hypothesis of metrical scholarship', not 'fixed: initial syllable'.

Nothing on accent, stress or syncope; bibliography only.
